title: Helping Civilians Understand Your Military Resume (We Checked 5,400 Profiles)
summary: A recruiter's guide built on 5,400 Simplify profiles: turn ranks into job titles, cut military acronyms and find civilian jobs that match your service.
body_markdown:
Translate the job, not the uniform. A recruiter needs to understand three things from your resume quickly: what you did, how big it was, and what you want to do next. Military resumes usually nail the second one. The first and third are where they lose people.


I lead recruiting and employer branding at Simplify, and I spent 17 years in engineering before I moved to this side of the table. When a military resume lands in my stack, it's often the one I end up reading twice. Not because the experience is thin. Usually it's the opposite. I read it twice because I have to decode it first, and most recruiters won't give it that second pass.


So we looked at how people describe military service on Simplify. Below is what we found in the work history of about 5,400 Simplify profiles that list military service, the changes I'd make to most of them, and which civilian jobs have the most openings right now.


## What do military resumes usually get right and wrong?


About 5,400 Simplify profiles list a role in the US Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, Space Force, National Guard or reserves, about 7,800 military roles in total. A few things stood out:


- **Most titles don't include a rank.** Only 10% of military role titles include a rank word like "Sergeant" or "Petty Officer." The rest name the job, though often in military terms, like "Infantryman" or "Squad Leader."
- **They're good with numbers.** 21% of military role descriptions say how many people the person led ("led 12 soldiers," "supervised 30 personnel"). For civilian jobs on the same profiles, it's 3%. Military roles also mention dollar amounts more often, 21% vs 12%.
- **About 1 in 10 still uses military-only acronyms.** The most common: COMSEC, GCSS, SIGINT, NCOIC, CBRN, SIPR, NIPR and OPSEC.
- **The gap is often long.** Among profiles where the military role had ended and a civilian job came after it (about 3,500), the median gap was 8 months. About a third started within a month. 40% took more than a year.


Two takeaways. The hard part is already done: you have scope and numbers, often more than a typical civilian resume. What holds military resumes back is mostly vocabulary. And a recruiter can't give you credit for something they can't read.


One honest caveat: Simplify's users lean toward tech and early-career jobs, so this is a picture of Simplify profiles, not every veteran. And it's based on the job history people entered on their Simplify profile, not on their actual resume files. The patterns are still worth knowing.


## How do you translate a military job title for a civilian resume?


Recruiters skim titles first. When I screen, the first thing I look at is the most recent title, and "Staff Sergeant" tells me your rank, not your job. Lead with what the work was. If you want the rank on there, and I think it's worth keeping, put it in parentheses.


**Before:** Staff Sergeant, US Army


**After:** Logistics Supervisor (Staff Sergeant), US Army


Not sure what your job is called outside the military? Look up your code on[My Next Move for Veterans](https://www.mynextmove.org/vets/find/military?ref=blog.simplify.jobs) . It's free, sponsored by the US Department of Labor, and it lists the civilian jobs that match each military code.


A quick story on why this matters. One of the best engineers I worked with in my engineering years came out of Air Force aircraft maintenance. He told me later that his first resume read like a maintenance log, full of system names and unit numbers, and it went nowhere. Once he rewrote it around what he actually did (diagnosing complex systems under time pressure, with zero room for error), he started getting calls.


## Should you use military acronyms on a resume?


The first time I saw "NCOIC" on a resume, I had to look it up. Most recruiters won't. Each acronym is a small speed bump, and three in a row is usually where a skim turns into a pass.


For every acronym, ask: would a hiring manager at this company know it? If not, spell it out or describe what it was for.


**Before:** NCOIC of COMSEC account; maintained SIPR/NIPR systems and ran OPSEC training.


**After:** Led the unit's secure communications program; maintained classified and unclassified computer networks and trained 40 people on information security.


Keep acronyms civilians use too, like IT, HR, QA and SOP, and certifications like CompTIA Security+.


**Your clearance is a special case.** On a resume you send directly to a defense company or government contractor for a job that needs one, an active clearance can be the line that moves you to the "call" pile, because getting someone cleared takes time and money. List the level and whether it's active, and that's it. Keep it off public versions, like your LinkedIn profile or resumes posted on open job boards. Security officials warn that advertising a clearance publicly makes you a target, and your agency or security officer may have its own rules, so check with them first.


## How do you quantify military experience on a resume?


You're already ahead here. The fix is to make each number point to an outcome, not just a responsibility.


**Before:** Responsible for 12 soldiers and $2M of equipment.


**After:** Led a 12-person maintenance team and kept $2M of vehicles and equipment at 95% readiness for 18 months.


The second version answers the question I'm really asking: if we hire this person, what will they get done? (These are example bullets. Use your real numbers.)


For how many bullets to write per job, we[counted 11,819 jobs on Simplify resumes](https://simplify.jobs/blog/how-many-bullet-points-per-job-resume?ref=blog.simplify.jobs) .


## Which civilian jobs match your military experience?


"I can do almost anything" is true of a lot of veterans, and it makes for the hardest resume to read. Pick the kind of role you want, then cut or shrink whatever doesn't support it. If you want two kinds of jobs, make two resumes.

Pay is the median annual pay posted on the entry-level full-time roles in each area that list pay (from 65 roles for cybersecurity to about 5,100 for security). It's what employers posted, not what veterans were actually paid.


Now look at the entry-level column. Security, warehouse, field service and driving have thousands of entry-level openings, but they pay less. Cybersecurity, IT, data and project management pay more, but only a few hundred of their roles are entry level.


So if you're aiming at those, my advice is not to apply as a beginner. Leading a team, owning equipment and working under pressure count as real experience. Write your resume around that, and apply to roles that ask for 2 to 5 years, not only the ones labeled entry level. The worst that happens is a no.


Simplify's free[resume builder](https://simplify.jobs/resume-builder?ref=blog.simplify.jobs) makes it easy to keep one version per job type.


## How do you explain the gap after leaving the military?


On Simplify profiles, the median gap between the end of a military role and the start of the next civilian job was 8 months, and 40% of those gaps were more than a year. Profiles don't say why, but school is probably part of it: about 1 in 10 started their civilian career with an internship.


A gap isn't a problem on its own. Just don't leave it blank. If you were in school, list it. If you were getting certified, list that.


If you're still serving, start before you leave. DoD SkillBridge lets you do approved training, an apprenticeship or an internship with a civilian employer during your last 180 days of service, while the military keeps paying you. Your command has to approve it, and how long you can go depends on your service and your unit's needs, so don't count on the full 180 days. The official[SkillBridge site](https://skillbridge.osd.mil/?ref=blog.simplify.jobs) has a searchable list of approved programs.


## What jobs do veterans get after the military?


Among the about 3,500 Simplify profiles with a civilian job listed after the military role, the most common next jobs were in software and engineering (18%), project and operations management (11%), IT (8%), sales and customer roles (8%), and technician, trades and warehouse work (7%).


Again, Simplify leans toward tech, so the software number is higher than you'd see across all veterans. But it's a useful reminder that people make big jumps out of the military. Your next job doesn't have to look like your last one.


## Common questions


**Should I put my rank on my resume?** Yes, but not as your job title. Lead with a civilian title like "Logistics Supervisor" and put the rank in parentheses. On Simplify, only 10% of military role titles include a rank word.


**Should I put my security clearance on my resume?** On resumes you send directly for jobs that need one, yes: list the level and that it's active. Keep it off public profiles and open job boards, and follow your agency's or security officer's rules.


**How do I translate my MOS into a civilian job title?** Look up your code on[My Next Move for Veterans](https://www.mynextmove.org/vets/find/military?ref=blog.simplify.jobs) , a free site sponsored by the US Department of Labor. Pick your branch, type in your MOS, rating or AFSC, and it lists similar civilian careers. For example,[Army 92Y, Unit Supply Specialist](https://www.mynextmove.org/vets/find/military?s=92Y&ref=blog.simplify.jobs) , matches shipping, receiving and inventory clerk, order clerk and purchasing agent, and at higher pay grades, wholesale and retail buyer. Stick to the first group of results, the careers that match most of your duties, because the longer list further down is much looser. Then turn the career name into a normal job title ("Inventory Specialist," not "Shipping, Receiving, & Inventory Clerks") that matches the job you're applying for.


**How long does it take veterans to find a civilian job?** On Simplify profiles with a civilian job listed after a military role, the median gap was 8 months. About a third started within a month, and 40% were more than a year. Profiles don't say why, but school is likely part of it.


**Do I include my DD-214?** For most private-sector jobs, no. Don't attach it to your resume; employers who need proof of service will ask. Federal jobs are different: if you're claiming veterans' preference on USAJOBS, you usually have to upload your DD-214 (the Member 4 copy is best) or other proof with the application, and some agencies will disqualify you if it's missing. Check each job announcement's required documents.


**How long should a military-to-civilian resume be?** One page if you have less than about 10 years of experience, two pages if you have more. If you're over, cut duties that don't relate to the job you want before you cut results.


**Which civilian jobs have the most entry-level openings for veterans?** On Simplify on November 9, 2026, warehouse and fulfillment had about 7,300 entry-level full-time roles open, security about 6,700, maintenance and repair about 5,300, field service about 4,000 and truck driving about 3,500. Their median posted pay runs $41,000 to $60,000 a year.


**Which civilian jobs pay the most for people leaving the military?** Among the areas we looked at, the median posted pay for entry-level roles was about $108,000 in cybersecurity (based on 65 roles that list pay), $90,000 in data and analytics and $75,000 in project management. That's what employers posted, not what veterans earned. And each area had only a few hundred entry-level openings on Simplify, so apply to roles that ask for a few years of experience too.


**Can I get a software or tech job after the military?** Yes. On Simplify profiles, software and engineering was the most common area for the first civilian job after the military, at 18%. Simplify's users lean toward tech, so the share across all veterans is likely lower.


**How do I show military leadership on a civilian resume?** Say how many people you led and what changed because of it, like "Led a 12-person team that..." On Simplify profiles, 21% of military roles already state a team size, compared with 3% of civilian jobs on the same profiles. Keep doing that.


**Should I list military awards and medals?** List the ones that show results, and add a few plain words on what each was for. A recruiter won't know what an award means unless you tell them.


**Should I put SkillBridge on my resume?** Yes. List it like any other role, with the company name, what kind of program it was (training, apprenticeship or internship) and what you did.


**I'm in the National Guard or reserves and have a civilian job. How do I list both?** List them as two separate jobs, each with its own dates. Recruiters are used to seeing them overlap.
